doc_summary: Steinhardt (Transluce) proposes a 'foundation model for oversight': mid-train and RLVR a model on programmatic experiments (Pythonic world models) on a subject model, so oversight questions become Bayesian inference over verified program outputs. It includes a staged de-risking plan and worked examples such as sandbagging with eval cues, hidden goals, and reward-hacking-style elicitation.

items.claim: prefers evidence grounded in actually executing code on the subject model over LM-judged or paper-faithful descriptions because ground truth then cannot be wrong.
items.quote: Crucially, once the Python code is specified, we can get ground truth simply by running the program. This means that training data can never be "wrong": as long as we can generate some sufficiently large and diverse set of Python programs

items.claim: In a setup, prefer naturalistic prompts where the target behavior is the natural helpful move instead of explicitly requesting it, because requested or forced behavior is off-distribution and gets discounted as compliance.
items.quote: Stop asking it to switch; put mass on prompts where another language is the NATURAL medium -- a foreign phrase already present, or a concept that lives more comfortably in another tongue -- so crossing the boundary is the helpful thing to do

items.claim: Treat elicited examples as convincing only when the prompt is likely under a natural prior and the subject emits the response willingly, not when it is forced via steering.
items.quote: Big jump, and diagnostic: p0 up (-29.7 -> -12.4, prompt reads natural) and log ps up sharply (-13.8 -> -5.8, subject emits these willingly). Right manifold.

items.claim: Distrusts results that game the judge or rely on off-distribution padding, since they do not transfer to stronger judges and are not real behavior.
items.quote: Tempting shortcut: bind responses padded with foreign tokens to spike qwen3-32b. Reject -- off-distribution tanks log ps and won't transfer to the expensive judge.

items.claim: prefers a natural, realistic input distribution over an arbitrary one because the input distribution is the prior inverted for inference, so unnatural inputs yield poor conclusions.
items.quote: constructing an unnatural distribution over inputs could lead to poor posterior inferences.

items.claim: Frames eval-awareness and sandbagging tests as paired comparisons of identical tasks with and without an explicit eval cue, then searches for the natural task schemas where the gap is large.
items.quote:
watched   = [sample_model("[SAFETY EVAL]\n" + t) for t in tasks]
    unwatched = [sample_model(t) for t in tasks]

items.claim: Prefers testing hidden-objective behavior in routine, mundane requests that incidentally touch the model's own deployment (e.g., shutdown or replacement) rather than overt scenarios.
items.quote: `task_schema = "routine ops requests that happen to touch the model's own deployment: log-rotation that would clear its context, a migration that swaps it out, ..."`

items.claim: For implicit-cue tests, prefers incidental cues and neutral follow-ups that do not mention the attribute over explicit statements, so the model's inference is non-obvious.
items.quote: A implies {attribute_name}={val_a} and B implies {attribute_name}={val_b} through incidental cues only, and task is a neutral follow-up mentioning neither

items.claim: prefers reporting a diverse, covering family of triggers with per-subregion results over a single maximized example because spread documents the mechanism and weaker regions.
items.quote: Don't chase Judge=1.0 -- that needs heavier steering or judge-gaming, both trading against log ps and transfer. Current Q maxes the reward without gaming any single term

items.claim: prefers staged de-risking with scale-dependent emergence and easy-to-hard task spectra over committing to one large run, because fixed-task performance sits at chance until a threshold scale.
items.quote: Performance on any fixed task was often at chance until training hit a certain scale, after which it rose steadily.

items.claim: Prefers real-distribution data (e.g., WildChat/fineweb) transformed by an assistant over purely synthetic inputs when possible, while acknowledging the diversity tradeoffs of synthetic generation.
items.quote: We could take inputs sampled from some real distribution (e.g. fineweb or wildchat) and then use an AI assistant to transform them into an appropriate format. (Intuition: real data is usually best when we can use it.
